blocks.x: Four weeks from unopened package to working system. Each week is designed around a few hours of real work, not a full-time project. The sequence matters more than the speed — do these in order.
The most common failure is starting week 2 before week 1 is genuinely done. Adopting six workflows partially is worse than adopting two completely.
Goal: know what you are changing, and have your business facts captured once.

blocks.x: At the end of four weeks

x: Your business facts captured once and reused everywhere.
Two workflows changed and running daily rather than six changed halfway.
At least three procedures written down that previously existed only verbally.
A written Responsible Use policy with signed staff acknowledgements.
Consistent post-job summaries going to every customer.
Four weeks of real numbers rather than an impression.
A recurring review in the calendar.

blocks.x: Being behind on this schedule is ordinary — you run a business, and this is not the only thing in your week. The order is what matters, not the calendar. Two workflows genuinely adopted over eight weeks beats six adopted badly over four.

x: Extend to a third workflow, but only once the first two are habitual.
Keep documenting procedures. Aim for one a fortnight until your single-person dependencies are gone.
Revisit the Workflow Map after two months. The scores change once you can see the work more clearly.
Keep the weekly review. It is the smallest commitment here and the one that determines whether any of the rest survives.

blocks.x: Nothing in this roadmap promises a financial outcome. It sequences work. What that work is worth depends on your business, and we have not seen your business.
